title: The Dinner Table Deal
tagline: Young children notice how it feels when a screen interrupts time together, act it out, and make a simple "table deal" with their family about one screen-free time, so everyone, grown-ups too, gets a turn to be listened to.
groupSize: Whole class, then taken home to make with the family
overview: Little kids feel it when a grown-up's eyes slide to a phone in the middle of their story, and grown-ups feel it when a child won't look up from a tablet at dinner. This lesson gives young children gentle words for that feeling and a tiny, fair plan to fix it. Children act out two short scenes, one where a screen interrupts time together and one where it doesn't, and notice the difference in their bodies and feelings. They learn that this is not about screens being bad; screens help us a lot, and there is a right time for them. Then they take home a "table deal": one screen-free time the whole family picks together, where everyone, kids and grown-ups, puts devices away so they can really listen to each other. The deal is on purpose a two-way promise, because children learn balance best when the adults they love practice it too.
objectives: Students will name how it feels to be interrupted by a screen and how it feels to be listened to.
Students will act out and tell the difference between screen-free together time and interrupted time.
Students will help their family choose one screen-free time and a kind way to ask for it.
Students will explain that the deal is for everyone in the family, grown-ups too.

print: Handout A: Two Scenes, picture cards to act out (1 teacher set, enlarged)
Handout B: How Did It Feel? (1 per student, or 1 enlarged for the class)
Handout C: Our Family Table Deal (1 per student, sent home)
Crayons; a pretend phone (a block or a card) for role-play
digital: Optional: a document camera to show the scene cards
Optional: a family may snap a photo of the finished deal to keep, no child's face needed

prep: Print and enlarge Handout A's two scene cards and Handout B for modeling.
Print Handout C for every child to take home.
Have a pretend phone ready (a wooden block, a folded card) so no real device is needed.
Read the family note on Handout C and add your name so families know who to contact.

steps.title: The slide-away eyes
steps.body: Start telling the class an exciting little story, then stop halfway and pretend to stare at a block in your hand like a phone. Wait a few seconds. Ask: **"How did that feel when my eyes went away?"** Let children say it: "sad," "you weren't listening," "I wanted you to look." Say warmly: "That is a real feeling. Today we're going to find a kind way to help everybody get listened to, kids and grown-ups."
steps.note: Children will instantly recognize this. Keep it playful, not shaming. The feeling of being half-listened-to is the whole hook.

steps.title: Two scenes
steps.body: Using Handout A, act out two short scenes with volunteers. **Scene 1:** a family at dinner where one person keeps looking at a pretend phone; the others try to share news. **Scene 2:** the same dinner, but the phone is in a basket and everyone listens. After each, ask the actors and the watchers: **"How did your body feel? How did your feelings feel?"** Fill in Handout B together with faces or words for each scene.
steps.note: Both kids and grown-ups can be the one on the phone in Scene 1, switch it, so children see it is a family habit, not just a kid problem.

steps.title: A kind way to ask
steps.body: Teach a gentle sentence anyone in the family can use: **"I want to hear you, so I'm putting my phone away."** And a way to ask for it: **"Can we have phones away so I can tell you something?"** Practice in pairs: one child asks kindly, the partner answers, "Yes, I'm listening," and puts the pretend phone in a basket. Remind them grown-ups can say it too, and it feels good to be the one who gets listened to.
steps.note: Give the exact words. Young children follow a script; "be kind about phones" is too abstract, but "I want to hear you" they can actually say at home.

steps.title: Start our table deal
steps.body: Children begin Handout C: draw the one time their family could make screen-free (dinner, bath time, the drive to school, bedtime stories). Draw where the phones will wait (a basket, a shelf). Draw everyone's faces listening. Circulate and ask, **"When is your family's listening time? Who puts their phone away, just you or grown-ups too?"** Help them see the answer is everyone.
steps.note: Keep choices flexible. Some families don't eat dinner together; "the car," "bedtime," or "breakfast" are all fine screen-free times.

steps.title: Listening feels like…
steps.body: In a circle, each child says one word for how it feels to be really listened to ("happy," "important," "warm"). Close together: **"Screens are good. People need listening too. Our deal is for everybody."** Tell children to finish the deal at home and bring back how it went.
steps.note: End on the balanced note: screens aren't the villain. The deal protects a little listening time; it does not ban devices.

unplugged: The whole lesson is unplugged: role-play with a pretend phone, a feelings chart, and a drawn family deal. A block or folded card stands in for a device, which keeps the focus on the feeling of being listened to, with no real screen in the room.
digital: If a family wants, they can take a photo of their finished table deal to keep on the fridge or a parent's phone as a reminder, with no child's face needed. A class could also make a shared drawing of "listening time" ideas to project, built only from children's pictures.
whyTech: This is best unplugged. The learning is about noticing feelings and practicing kind words face to face, and a real device would pull attention toward the screen, which is exactly what the lesson asks everyone to set aside for a moment.

adaptations.label: Kindergarten
adaptations.text: Do only Scene 1 and Scene 2 and the feelings chart with faces; children draw just the screen-free time, no words needed.

adaptations.label: Grade 2
adaptations.text: Add a sentence on the deal: children write the kind words their family will use and one thing they'll do instead during listening time.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Teach the kind sentence in the child's home language too, and let children answer the feelings chart with faces or colors.

adaptations.label: Children in different family settings
adaptations.text: Use "the people I live with" instead of assuming a dinner table, and let any shared moment (a bus ride, a bedtime) be the screen-free time.

lookFors: Children name a feeling for being interrupted by a screen and a feeling for being listened to.
Children act out or describe the difference between the interrupted scene and the listening scene.
The table deal names one screen-free time, where phones wait, and that grown-ups join too.
Children use or recall a kind sentence for asking to be listened to.
reflection: How does it feel when someone really listens to you? (Student ELE 3.2: I communicate my ideas clearly to others.)
Why is it fair for grown-ups to put their phones away too? (Student ELE 3.3: I value diverse perspectives in group work.)
What will your family do together during your screen-free time?
transfer: Children finish the table deal at home with their family and try it for a few days, then share in a class circle one thing that felt good and one thing that was hard. Families are encouraged to keep the deal and change the time if a different one fits better.

handouts.title: Two Scenes
handouts.instructions: Act these out with a pretend phone (a block or card). After each scene, talk about how it felt.

cards.label: scene 1
cards.front: Dinner time. One person keeps looking at a phone. The others try to tell about their day, but the phone keeps pulling the eyes away.
cards.back: Ask: How did it feel for the people trying to share? For the person on the phone? (Let a grown-up be the one on the phone sometimes.)

cards.label: scene 2
cards.front: Same dinner. The phone is resting in a basket. Everyone looks at each other and listens. One person shares good news and everyone hears it.
cards.back: Ask: How did this feel different? What did your body do? What did your feelings do?

cards.label: try it
cards.front: A child wants to show a grown-up a picture they drew, but the grown-up is scrolling. Act out a kind way to ask for listening.
cards.back: Practice: "Can we have phones away so I can show you something?" The grown-up says, "Yes, I'm listening," and puts the phone down.

cards.label: try it
cards.front: A grown-up wants to hear about a child's day, but the child is deep in a tablet game. Act out a kind way to ask for listening.
cards.back: Practice: "I want to hear about your day. Let's put screens away for a little." Everyone gets a turn to ask and to listen.

cards.label: both ways
cards.front: Show a moment where a screen HELPED the family (a video call with a far-away grandparent, a recipe, a song to dance to).
cards.back: Remember: screens are good and help us a lot. The deal is only about one listening time, not about screens being bad.

cards.label: both ways
cards.front: Show the family choosing their listening time together and everyone putting phones in the basket, grown-ups too.
cards.back: The deal is for EVERYBODY. That is what makes it fair and easy to keep.

handouts.title: How Did It Feel?
handouts.instructions: After each scene, draw a face or write a word. There are no wrong answers. Just notice how it felt.

handouts.title: Our Family Table Deal
handouts.instructions: Start at school. Finish at home with your family. Family note: this is not about screens being bad, they help us a lot. It is a two-way promise to protect one listening time where EVERYONE, grown-ups too, puts devices away. Please make this deal together with your child.

sections.prompt: Draw the one time our family will make screen-free so we can listen to each other (dinner, bedtime, the car, breakfast).
Draw where the phones will wait during our listening time (a basket, a shelf, another room).
The kind words we will use: "I want to hear you, so I'm putting my phone away."
Everyone who promises to join the deal (kids AND grown-ups):
